entries.title: How prepared is Kenya for an Ebola outbreak?
entries.summary: The first confirmed Ebola cases in Kenya have raised urgent questions about the country's public health preparedness and border controls. But the health ministry says there is no need for panic.
entries.content:
October 16, 2026

The first confirmed Ebola cases in Kenya have raised urgent questions about the country's public health preparedness and border controls. But the health ministry says there is no need for panic.

Kenyais rushing to contain Ebola linked to the deadliest outbreak on record in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) . The East African nation has reported two cases and one death, while the DRC has reported over 9,000 cases and 4,400 deaths.

Kenya's first Ebola patient died at Nairobi hospital on October 5. The 40-year-old Kenyan had traveled by road from the DRC to Uganda before boarding a flight to Nairobi in Entebbe on October 3. 

One of his relatives is now confirmed to have contracted the virus. The 39-year-old was under quarantine when he developed symptoms on October 13. "Both cases are linked, and ​there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," Kenya's health ministry said.

Contact tracing has been ongoing since officials first detected the case. Of the 128 people who came into contact with the first Ebola patient, 113 have been identified, according to the health ministry. All, except five—who are in unspecified countries abroad—have been quarantined. 

Should Kenyans worry about Ebola spreading?

Public anxiety is rising, with fears of lockdowns and economic disruption and skepticism about government readiness.

"It's a very dangerous disease, so it's very shocking," a Nairobi resident told DW.  Another citizen said he was disappointed: "The government has been caught unaware. It appears to me that the government was not prepared, especially at the entry point of this particular person who was found to be suffering from Ebola." 

One woman said she felt there was a lack of public information on the disease. "The government should do more in educating and sensitizing about it, and raising awareness," she said.

Kenya's Health Ministry, through its Cabinet Secretary, Aden Duale, has been seeking to allay fears, urging Kenyans to remain vigilant and encouraging anyone who develops symptoms to report to the nearest medical facility. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), symptoms can develop between 2 and 21 days after infection.

Early symptoms include: fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat. Later, a patient may suffer from vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and kidney and liver infection.

However, these symptoms might be similar to other illnesses such as malaria or typhoid, and only an Ebola test can confirm if one has been exposed to the virus.

Criticism and calls to improve screening

Several prominent figures, medical unions and opposition politicians have criticized Kenya's response to its first Ebola cases. Former Chief Justice David Maraga, who has declared interest in running for the presidency in the 2027 election, questioned how a man carrying the Ebola virus could pass through screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, Nairobi. 

"We don't know how many have been infected. We must demand appropriate action be taken so that we don't have deaths arising from that disease," Maraga told The Standard.

Kalonzo Musyoka, Kenya's vice president from 2008 to 2013, meanwhile noted that doctors at Nairobi Hospital, not border systems, detected the danger.

Dr. Dennis Miskellah of the Kenya Medical Practitioners, Pharmacists and Dentists Union believes that the Ebola cases show that Kenya's health system is not pandemic-ready. "This system is not yet resilient. This system did not learn from the COVID pandemic that we had a few years ago," he said. 

"Since May, we've had this outbreak in the region. Uganda, our immediate neighbor, had almost 20 cases. So, we had ample time to prepare adequately. But it seems like somebody dropped the ball."

Kenya went on high alert after the DRC declared the Ebola outbreak in May. The government designated several hospitals as isolation centers.

It also enhanced screening at airports and border points, deploying mobile labs. Flights from several African countries were ordered to land in designated airport wings for screening.

Where are the gaps in Kenya's health system?

"Top of it all is that there's has been a serious lapse of leadership in governance of healthcare this country," said Miskellah. "All those broken pillars, there's no clear responsibility or chain of command, whether its the Ministry of Health or the 47 county governments who are semi-automous."

Capacity at some isolation centers is limited. Rural facilities lack resources such as the protective gear available at major hospitals, according to Miskellah. And there's also a shortage of health workers due to a freeze on public service workers.

Meanwhile, healthcare workers, many of whom have no healthcare cover, are reportedly wary of putting their lives at risk. Dozens of Kenyan nurses and doctors lost their lives during the COVID-19 pandemic. 

Kenya's agreements on Ebola with its neighbors are being called into question since the first case was recorded in Kenya, which has one of the strongest healthcare systems in the region.

Experts are questioning the state of regional cooperation on Ebola, where borders have largely remained open despite the surge in cases and deaths. "Before we trust these agreements and cooperation, then we have have to audit them and question them so that we don't just blindly believe that Kenya is doing the right thing, or that the DRC is doing the right thing," said Miskellah.

Then, there's the question of individual responsibility. Kenya requires travelers arriving from Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, Zambia, Rwanda, Burundi, Central African Republic and South Sudan to complete a health declaration form — truthfully.

Adapted from the Africalink Podcast by Benita van Eyssen.

entries.title: Italy cuts air traffic in half amid data transmission issue
entries.summary: Citing problems with the data transmission network, Italian authorities have drastically reduced the volume of flights in their airspace. The ENAV authority ruled out malicious activity and said flights remained safe.
entries.content:
Italy

Italy cuts air traffic in half amid data transmission issue

October 16, 2026

Citing problems with the data transmission network, Italian authorities have drastically reduced the volume of flights in their airspace. The ENAV authority ruled out malicious activity and said flights remained safe.

Air travelers across Italy faced delays and cancellations on Friday because of a problem with the country's air traffic control systems. 

The ENAV air traffic control authority ruled out foul play such as a cyberattack, and said it was forced to introduce temporary restrictions of the volume of flights after identifying a data transmission problem.

Major aiports in cities like Rome and Milan warned of likely disruptions and advised passengers to check with their airlines. 

What did authorities say about the problem?

ENAV said it first identified the issue overnight. It was forced to restrict the volume of flights at around 6 a.m. (0400 GMT/UTC) as the number of scheduled services increased.

"We would like to inform you that this morning we guaranteed the greatest possible number of departures, including intercontinental flights," ENAV said.

Shorter-distance services were more likely to be interrupted.

"Despite the anomalies encountered on the data transmission network, we are deploying all avaialable resources to minimize disruption and restore full operations as soon as possible," ENAV said. "We confirm an operational capacity of 50% of total air traffic, ensuring maximum safety at all times, which remains the Company's top priority."

ENAV said it had ruled out the possibility of the disturbance being caused by "malicious acts."

Rome airports operator ADR warned passengers that "flight delays and cancellations may occur" and advised passengers to contact their airline if uncertain. Milan airports company SEA issued a similar notice.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Germany, France agree deal to support European car industry
entries.summary: The two countries said the agreement aimed to safeguard Europe's automative industry, encouraging development and research. Car makers in Europe have so far struggled to compete with Chinese electric car companies.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany, France agree deal to support Europe's struggling car industry

October 16, 2026

The two countries said the agreement aimed to safeguard Europe's automative industry, encouraging development and research. Car makers in Europe have so far struggled to compete with Chinese electric car companies.

Germany and France have agreed a deal to protect Europe's automotive industry, the countries said in a statement Friday.

The plan aims to cut CO2 emissions and support the development and construction of electric cars in Europe, the statement added.

"Our shared ambition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe," the countries said.

The pact also includes incentives for investment, research and production.

Tough competition from China

European car makers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market,  resulting in cost-cutting measures.

Premier of the state of Lower Saxony Olaf Lies hailed the agreement as a "strong signal" in support of Europe's car industry that protects jobs in the sector.

Lower Saxony is where German automotive giantVolkswagen's headquarters are located, in the city of Wolfsburg.  Lies is also part of VW's supervisory board.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Clashes erupt at Argentine student protests against President Milei's austerity policies
entries.summary: Demonstrators clashed with police as President Javier Milei's decision not to release funding for universities brought students and employees to the streets. Protesters say the country's future is at stake.
entries.content:
October 16, 2026

Demonstrators clashed with police as President Javier Milei's decision not to release funding for universities brought students and employees to the streets. Protesters say the country's future is at stake.

Protesters took to the streets in Argentina's capital, Buenos Aires, to demonstrate against libertarian President Javier Milei's cost-cutting measures for education.

Thousands of students, university staff, trade unionists and opposition supporters crowded outside the parliament, demanding the implementation of a law to finance universities.

While the rally was largely peaceful, clashes also erupted, with reports of masked individuals throwing stones at police, injuring at least eight officers. Some 25 people were arrested, according to the country's National Security Ministry.

Reports said other protesters had tried to push those throwing stones back. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.

Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva said the protesters wanted to "sow chaos," posting on her X account that the right to protest is not "a right to exercise violence."

Milei vetoes law, refuses to release funding

This was the fifth protest over the Milei government's education spending to take place since Milei entered office in 2023.Such a demonstration also took place in May, in which organizers say some 1.5 million people took part.

Milei vetoed a law, passed by Congress in 2025, requiring the government to invest more money in public universities.

The University Funding Law says the state should increase employees' salaries in line with inflation dated to December 2023. It also calls for the restoration of student scholarships and more funding for universities' operations.

Congress subsequently overrode Milei's veto, and several court rulings have instructed the government to release the funds, but it has so far refused to do so.

According to Milei, who was elected after promising wide-ranging cost-cutting measures, justified his veto by saying "there is no money" for inflation-linked spending increases.

A government spokesperson said the law had been "suspended" due to the government's legal action against it.

The first half of 2026 saw public spending on universities fall by 41% in real terms, according to the Center for National Economic Research of the University of Buenos Aires.

Argentina's education system is considered to be among the best in South America. Study at public universities is free, drawing students from across the region.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Who was Eva Mamlok? Berlin square renamed after Jewish anti-fascist resistance fighter
entries.summary: She started taking action against Hitler as a teenager and never stopped until her death in a concentration camp. Berlin's Blücherplatz is now being renamed after her.
entries.content:
October 16, 2026

She started taking action against Hitler as a teenager and never stopped until her death in a concentration camp. Berlin's Blücherplatz is now being renamed after her.

In the history of German resistance to Nazism, some names have become symbols: Sophie Scholl, Claus von Stauffenberg, Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Georg Elser.

Yet many others have remained largely forgotten.

Among them is Eva Mamlok, a young Jewish woman from Berlin whose acts of defiance began in her teenage years and continued until her murder in a Nazi concentration camp.

Now more people will get to know her story as Berlin renames Blücherplatz, a square in the district of Kreuzberg, Eva-Mamlok-Platz on October 16.

"Eva Mamlok was a very remarkable person. As a young Jewish woman from Berlin, her spirit of resistance was particularly striking," says cultural researcher Alexandra Weltz-Rombach, who has worked extensively with the historians' network "Gruppe Eva Mamlok."

'Down with Hitler'

Eva Mamlok was born on May 6, 1918, into a Jewish family in Berlin. They ran a wholesale wine business, and the family belonged to the vibrant Jewish middle class that formed an important part of Berlin's social and economic life during the Weimar Republic.

But Eva came of age just as Germany was descending into dictatorship. When Hitler became chancellor in 1933, she was only 14 years old. She was also a member of the Socialist Workers' Youth (SAJ). Following the suppression of the left-wing political youth organization later that year, she became active in the underground resistance.

According to testimony from Inge Berner (1922-2012), the sole survivor of Mamlok's later resistance group, Eva climbed onto the roof of a department store on Blücherplatz as a teenager and painted the slogan "Down with Hitler."

"She was caught doing that, though she wasn't arrested at that particular moment — that didn't happen until a year later," notes Weltz-Rombach.

Arrested for honoring socialist icons Luxemburg and Liebknecht

Eva Mamlok first appeared in official records in November 1934, after she was arrested for taking part in commemorations for socialist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht at Berlin's Friedrichsfelde Cemetery.

Authorities determined that the 16-year-old held "hostile views toward the state" and placed her in "protective custody until further notice" — a euphemism the regime used to justify imprisonment without trial. She was sent to the women's concentration camp at Moringen in Lower Saxony, where she remained until May 1935.

After her release, she continued her anti-Nazi activities despite the increasing danger, facing persecution both as a political dissident and as a Jew.

In these underground circles, she met Pieter Siemsen (1914–2004), and they remained a couple until he emigrated to Argentina in 1937. The only known surviving photograph of Eva comes from his personal archive.

She had a daughter, Tana, in 1939. The father's identity is unknown, however. The child was placed in a Jewish orphanage in Berlin and deported in 1942 to the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp, where she was murdered.

Meanwhile, because she was Jewish, Eva Mamlok was forced to perform compulsory labor at the Berlin firm F. Butzke Schrauben-Industrie in 1940. There she met other women who shared her opposition to Nazism.

Together they formed what later became known as the "Eva Mamlok Group," an informal resistance network of Jewish and non-Jewish women. They distributed anti-Nazi leaflets and wrote slogans critical of Hitler.

They also shared banned books. "They were books that are today part of Germany's educational canon," from Thomas Mann to Lion Feuchtwanger, notes Weltz-Rombach. She adds that the fact that the Berlin Central and Regional Library (ZLB), Germany's largest public library, stands on the new Eva-Mamlok-Platz is a fitting symbol of this act of resistance and the importance of books.

Mamlok and others in her group were arrested for distributing this forbidden literature. On January 13, 1942, she was deported from Berlin to the Riga Ghetto in occupied Latvia.

According to Inge Berner's testimony, Mamlok remained active in the resistance there too. For example, she arranged for a contact still in Berlin to send her a cake with a miniature camera hidden inside it to document persecution in the ghetto.

In October 1944, she was sent to the Stutthof Nazi concentration camp, where she died in December of that year.

Replacing old symbols of Franco-German hostility

Blücherplatz was named after the Prussian field marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, whose most renowned achievement was leading his army against Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

Several places, including streets and parks, have been named after him in Germany.

"There is no shortage of Blücher memorial sites," says Weltz-Rombach. "And perhaps it's also time to put an end to this old Franco-German enmity — which is, of course, inherent in the name Blücher, given its Prussian tradition — and to establish, in its place, a different form of remembrance," she adds.

The square also happens to be the site of the Carnival of Cultures, a multicultural street festival and parade held every year to celebrate Berlin's global diversity.

Role models for a new generation

Having first heard about Mamlok when a Stolperstein commemorating her was laid in 2011, Weltz-Rombach has been researching her biography for the past few years. The Berlin-based filmmaker, producer and curator has also been sharing the resistance fighter's story through various projects, including an exhibition in 2024 and a podcast series with young Berliners.

Since Eva Mamlok was only a teenager herself when she became politically active, the workshop participants can easily relate to her fate.

These teenagers learn about Mamlok's experiences at the actual locations where she was active, helping them imagine what it would be like to be arrested and imprisoned for six months without trial for doing things that normally wouldn't be considered crimes — such as simply expressing an opinion publicly or laying flowers at a commemorative event, explains Weltz-Rombach.

"Above all, she is, of course, a role model — an example of how one would like to act oneself, and how courageous one would like to be."

Women's "resistance was often of a more everyday nature, rather than planting bombs," notes Weltz-Rombach. Their stories offer examples of "forms of resistance that have only recently received more attention." She mentions, for example, a 2024 exhibition and the launch of a database dedicated to female resistance fighters. 

Even though many of the eyewitnesses have now died, Weltz-Rombach believes there are still many more of these stories that deserve to be brought into the spotlight: "There are definitely many names we do not know, that are waiting to be further researched."

Edited by: Joshua Lang

entries.title: Europe promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China
entries.summary: At an international AI summit in Dublin, European leaders promoted trusted and independent AI. Critics question whether the EU can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation.
entries.content:
October 16, 2026

At an international AI summit in Dublin, European leaders promoted trusted and independent AI. Critics question whether the EU can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation.

If supremacy in artificial intelligence (AI) was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China. Europe, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the conversation.

Former president of the European Central Bank Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route Europe has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the EU controls little of the value chain.

"Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic."

Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its 6-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency.

The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister.

AI safety concerns shadow growth agenda

Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm.

Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pausein order for safety measures to catch up.

Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards.

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety.

"We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI."

AI critics say key concerns overlooked

Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act, requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers.

However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions. 

Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues.

"There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW.

"It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace."

Europe faces a widening AI gap

A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development.

Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US.

The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers.

As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event.

The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.

In keeping with Draghi's calls for Europe to develop its own AI sovereignty, particularly in supply chains and infrastructure, the declaration suggests that European firms reliant on non-EU cloud and computing services may face additional compliance pressures.

Can Europe balance innovation and regulation?

However, not everyone is convinced by the EU's capacity to either ramp up AI capacity or develop effective regulation.

Eddie Wilson, CEO of European airline Ryanair, said he doubted Brussels could regulate AI well without stifling innovation.

"The last thing you want is people regulating this industry who don't know anything about it," he told DW. "That's generally what happens in Brussels."

Ryanair recently made a major deal with Google to use its cloud data system and its AI platform Gemini Enterprise. It's precisely the kind of collaboration with US AI supply chains that the EU says it wants companies to move away from.

"I worry for Europe because these tech companies need to move at speed," said Wilson. He believes the environment in the US is more amenable to innovation.

"If they're not going to do it here, they're going to do it elsewhere. They're going to do it in China and they're going to do it in the US."

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: Formula 1 in Rwanda: Sportswashing claims vs. hopes for African legacy
entries.summary: Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time since 1993. There is concern Rwanda are using it as another sportswashing opportunity, but there is also hope the event's legacy can impact wider African society.
entries.content:
October 16, 2026

Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time since 1993. There is concern Rwanda are using it as another sportswashing opportunity, but there is also hope the event's legacy can impact wider African society.

Rwanda's sports portfolio has grown after confirming it will host Formula One races from the early 2030s. The track is to be built in Bugesera near Kigali International Airport, which Qatar Airways, an F1 sponsor, owns 60% of.

"To be an African and to see it happening in real time, for me in my lifetime because Kyalami [the track in South Africa where F1 was last hosted in Africa] was before I was born, I'm more than happy to have it on the continent," South African presenter and content creator Nqobile Khwezi told Sky Sports.

"To be able to give that taste back to the rest of the world and the audience of Formula One would be an absolute delight."

F1 have also highlighted the benefits for the host nation.

"Through this race we have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to our more than 100 million fans across Africa and firmly believe that sport can be a positive force for good," an F1 spokesperson told The Athletic.

DW contacted Rwanda's Ministry of Sports for comment, but did not receive a promised reply.

Kagame continues ventures into sport

For the country's President, Paul Kagame, another move into sport is hardly a surprise given his ventures into European football and the NBA in recent years. Rwanda even sponsored Bayern Munich, but fan and media backlash over the deal caused the Bundesliga club to drop the commercial element with the country's tourist arm, Visit Rwanda, last year.

With many critics accusing Kagame and Rwanda of sportswashing, the arrival of F1, a sport valued at approximately $34 billion (€30 billion), according to sports business website Sportico, brings fresh questions.

"This deal may have positive economic and social impacts across Africa, but we should be realistic about circumstances on the ground in Rwanda," Lewis Mudge, Central Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told DW.

"Human Rights Watch wrote to Formula One in February 2025 to ask how it is addressing the human rights impacts of its activities, including regarding Rwanda and other countries’ bid to host a F1 Grand Prix. We did not receive a response," said Mudge, adding that F1 should only approve racing in the country after addressing the human rights impacts of hosting a race there.

"Rwanda, like other countries, has also used high-profile sports deals and races in the past to distract from its abysmal human rights record. Rwanda is currently the power behind the abusive M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and its military forces have been implicated in unlawful displacement and deaths of civilians in violation of international humanitarian law."

For Mohamed Keita, returning the sport to Africa is overdue, but the choice of country is telling.

"The fact that F1 excluded the world's second largest continent from its race series for three decades is indefensible in its own right and is actually a stain on a sport which claims to be global," Keita, Senior Policy Officer, Africa, at the Human Rights Foundation told DW.

"The choice of Rwanda, however, is deeply controversial," Keita continued. "Rwanda is a brutal dictatorship. Its regime is under partial US sanctions for its military occupations of territories of eastern DRC. Rwanda is arming and financing a militia involved in rapes, massacres, forced recruitment and violent plunder of natural resources."

Just Rwanda, or will F1 also come to South Africa?

Formula One has history on the continent. In 1958, there was a race in Morocco and more recently, in South Africa, where the last F1 race in Africa took place at the Kyalami racetrack in Johannesburg in 1993. Many previous races in the country were overshadowed by the policy of apartheid.

Despite Rwanda securing the deal first, South Africa believes it will host before them. When Rwanda announced their hosting, South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa sent his congratulations in a social media post, adding: "This contract is a recognition of the capabilities of the Rwandan nation and of our continent more broadly."

South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie also congratulated Rwanda, but pivotally added that South Africa "will get F1, even before 2030."

There is no denying that hosting a race in South Africa would cost significantly less time and money, given the existing infrastructure.

Event legacy opportunities also present

In either country, comes a legacy opportunity. Sports such as Formula One, where the majority of decision-makers, drivers, team principles and engineers are white men, are a living example of the unlevel playing field. The hope of racing in Africa is that it will go some way to changing that.

"I think that's the kind of aspirational drive of hosting a Formula 1 race. It's leveraging STEM [science, technology, engineering, and mathematics] education, technology, aspiring young girls or women, leveling the playing fields, if it's for all those other reasons and we can make it work then I say yes to Formula 1 in Africa," Dr. Kamilla Swart-Arries, an expert in South Africa's events industry and the legacy of sports events, told DW in 2024.

"I hope F1 will consider further investment in developing African talent in motorsport," said Keita. "There's a lot of good that F1 can do if it genuinely wants to grow the sport in Africa, but Rwanda does not make sense at this moment unless you're doing it purely for the benefit of one dictator and the beauty of the hilly terrain."

"The proposition here is to take the world's most expensive sport to Rwanda, which is one of the world's poorest countries. Rwanda is consistently listed among the UN's list of the 25 least developed countries in the world," said Keita.

The return of the fastest show in sports is a huge moment for both Rwanda and Africa. It raises questions about President Kagame's use of sport, but it also offers an opportunity to shape the event's legacy. Unlike the race Rwanda wants to host, this is not about being the fastest but about making the most of the chance.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

entries.title: California wildfires force evacuations near Malibu
entries.summary: A fast-moving fire near Malibu has forced evacuations. Stronger overnight winds threaten to spread the flames further.
entries.content:
United States of America

California wildfires force evacuations near Malibu

October 16, 2026

A fast-moving fire near Malibu has forced evacuations. Stronger overnight winds threaten to spread the flames further.

Several brush fires burned across southern California on Friday, forcing evacuations near Malibu as hot, dry winds fueled the flames.

The rapidly spreading Bryson Fire grew to about 81 hectares (200 acres) and threatened a Los Angeles County juvenile detention and rehabilitation facility, which was evacuated Thursday night.

What is happening near Malibu?

Authorities ordered residents to leave the Encinal Canyon area near Malibu, a coastal town west of Los Angeles. Surrounding parts of the Santa Monica Mountains were placed under evacuation warnings.

The National Weather Service forecast stronger gusts overnight that could intensify the fires.

The Bryson Fire was first reported around 5 p.m. local time Thursday (0000 GMT Friday), north of Malibu. A large plume of dark smoke rose above the hills and could be seen from miles away.

Los Angeles County officials urged residents to follow emergency instructions and check on neighbors who might need help, if safe to do so.

"If you feel unsafe due to a fire nearby ... do not wait for an official alert to leave," officials said.

The blaze was burning about 32 kilometers (20 miles) west of the area devastated by the Palisades Fire in January 2025.

Where else are firefighters battling blazes?

In Azusa, north of Los Angeles, about 200 firefighters tackled a wind-driven fire that burned more than 16 hectares (40 acres).

Crews stopped its forward spread by mid-afternoon, and evacuation orders for a neighborhood in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains were downgraded to warnings.

Further south, a fire at Camp Pendleton, a military base near San Diego, burned more than 3.8 square kilometers (1.5 square miles), threatening buildings and infrastructure.

Power companies cut supplies to about 127,000 customers across California to reduce the risk of electrical equipment sparking further fires.

The Palisades and Eaton fires killed 31 people in the Los Angeles area in January 2025. Forecasters said the current winds were not expected to reach the strength recorded during those disasters.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Wildfire kills 4 firefighters in Indonesia's Mount Bromo national park
entries.summary: The latest victims of Indonesia's wildfires were trapped by thick smoke and fast-spreading flames, authorities said. Meanwhile, the toxic haze from the fires has spread to Indonesia's neighbors.
entries.content:
Indonesia

Blaze kills 4 firefighters in Indonesia's Mount Bromo national park

October 16, 2026

The latest victims of Indonesia's wildfires were trapped by thick smoke and fast-spreading flames, authorities said. Meanwhile, the toxic haze from the fires has spread to Indonesia's neighbors.

At least four people have died and two others suffered severe burns while battling wildfires in a national park on Indonesia's main island, officials said on Friday.

They were trapped by thick smoke and fast-spreading flames in the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java, a Forestry Ministry statement said, as the country's worst wildfires in a decade swept through the area.

The southeast Asian country has been battling a months-long crisis of blazes and toxic smoke, forcing schools to shut down and causing a surge in respiratory complaints in the region.

The victims were part of a 12-member firefighting team consisting of national park personnel, members of the community fire brigade, and local volunteers, said East Java police spokesperson Jules Abraham Abast.

"This incident serves as a reminder that forest and land fire extinguishing is a high-risk operation," the ministry statement said, adding there had been a jump in hotspots detected by satellites as areas of unusually high temperatures. Not all hotspots necessarily translate into individual fires.

By Thursday evening, the number of hotspots in Indonesia stood at 799 , up from 372 a day earlier. The forest and land fires have worsened this year as weather phenomenon El Nino prolonged the dry season.

Toxic haze spreads across southeast Asia

The smoke from Indonesia's wildfires are causing a health crisis in neighboring southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.

Malaysia on Friday ordered hundreds of schools to close down due to deteriorating air quality.

Singapore, meanwhile, topped IQAir's live ranking of the world's most polluted major cities, with Kuala Lumpur second and Jakarta sixth.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan rejected calls from some lawmakers to seek compensation from Indonesia, saying the crisis should be addressed through diplomatic engagement and established mechanisms.

He said Malaysia was coordinating assistance for Indonesia and would push for stronger regional cooperation on haze management.

Singapore probing companies linked to fires

Singapore also called for closer cooperation. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said authorities were investigating companies allegedly linked to Indonesian forest and land fires that have worsened the haze.

"Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries," he said.

Singapore enacted the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014 after a bout of severe pollution.

The law allows authorities to target companies whose activities overseas cause or contribute to unhealthy haze levels in Singapore. That said, legal experts cautioned that pursuing companies under the law will be challenging.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: India's 'Cockroaches' to march again after protest crackdown
entries.summary: The Cockroach Janta Party has called on people to gather at New Delhi's central business district to wave the Indian national flag as it asserts a right to protest. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India's 'Cockroaches' to march again after protest crackdown

Published October 16, 2026last updated October 16, 2026

The Cockroach Janta Party has called on people to gather at New Delhi's central business district to wave the Indian national flag as it asserts a right to protest. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here are the latest developments from India on Friday, October 16:

  • The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) slated to hold 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave The Tricolor) rally
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi to visit Canada from December 11-12
  • Indian Embassy calls on nationals in Saudi Arabia to remain calm and alert amid intensifying Houthi strikes

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Police ask CJP's Dipke to call off Delhi march

Police ask CJP's Dipke to call off Delhi march

Delhi Police reached the house where Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke is staying in the capital and served him a notice barring him from holding the planned 'Tiranga' rally, just hours before the protest was set to begin, Indian media reports said.

The police told Dipke that prohibitory orders were already in force for the Connaught Place area, where the 'Cockroach' movement has asked people to gather with the Indian national flag.

Videos circulating on India media channels showed Dipke sitting with uniformed police officials, as an Indian flag is seen draped on his shoulders.

Dipke was reportedly told that waving the flag was not against the law, but a march without permission and an assembly of people would be a violation of the restrictions in place, making them liable to legal action.

Skip next section Reliance 'welcomes' Starlink competition amid Elon Musk's 'monopoly' salvo

Reliance 'welcomes' Starlink competition amid Elon Musk's 'monopoly' salvo

Indian business mogul Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries on Friday dismissed allegations that it was blocking Elon Musk'sStarlink satellite internet service in the country, saying that its own satellite services were awaiting clearance. 

"At Reliance, we have never feared competition. We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best," the company said as it went on to "welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink."

Starlink is operated by Musk's SpaceX and provides high-speed internet access to remote locations through low Earth orbit satellites.

Despite securing key licenses and signing distribution agreements with telecom giants Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel, Starlink remains in a regulatory limbo and is yet to begin commercial operations in the country.

The statement is Reliance's first reaction, following a public tirade on X by US trillionaire Musk, who claimed Ambani was hindering Starlink's years-long efforts to rollout in India.

Last week, Musk accused Ambani of a "monopolistic exploitation" of Indians and sarcastically called the Indian billionaire "Prime Minister Ambani."

"Please accept my humble apologies for not realizing that you are the real boss of India," Musk said as he addressed Ambani, directly.

"Would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?" he asked.

Reliance's Friday statement does not name Musk. The company said it wanted to place "the facts on record" in light of "recent remarks about Reliance and the Indian market."

After Musk's remarks, India's Ministry of Communication said the government maintained a" fair and non-discriminatory authorization framework" for all telecom services, without naming the SpaceX boss.

Skip next section CJP scheduled to hold 'Tiranga' rally at Delhi's Connaught Place with Indian flag

CJP scheduled to hold 'Tiranga' rally at Delhi's Connaught Place with Indian flag

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is set to hold a march on Friday in the Indian capital named "Lehra Do Tiranga," which translates to "wave the tricolor." Tricolor refers to the Indian national flag, which has saffron, white and green bands.

The rally comes in support of two of the movement's leaders — Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das — who were sent to a five-day detention in prison on Wednesday over charges including alleged trespassing, violation of prohibitory orders and breach of a peace bond. 

A video shared by the CJP on Tuesday showed its co-conveners Das and Ranka, along with other activists of the collective, climbing a gate cordoned off with yellow police barricades.

As they jumped to the other side of the gate, they were seen holding up the Indian flag and shouting slogans against India's election chief. The group is then seen being chased by police officials.

"Imagine being jailed in your own country for waving your own national flag," CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke wrote on X on Thursday.

CJP's Tuesday demonstration attempt took place at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, a day after the site was removed as the official protest venue of the capital.

It was also the same site where thousands of protesters attempted to march on October 10 to demand electoral reforms before being thwarted by Indian authorities.

Thousands of youth protesters, including CJP and student leaders, were detained after police denied permission to protest. The demonstrators have said that protest is a fundamental right.

The demonstrations are a part of a broader push —  including by opposition parties — for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the purging of tens of millions of names from India's electoral rolls. 

Skip next section Rogue AI agents accessed 'confidential' data of Indian firms, government says

Rogue AI agents accessed 'confidential' data of Indian firms, government says

Artificial Intelligence (AI) models under "research and evaluation" broke into Indian firms' live systems and read business records, including confidential material, the country's cybersecurity agency has revealed. 

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) highlighted the incidents in an advisory titled 'AI Agents as Attack Vectors.'

It is the first such official account in India and follows a series of incidents reported around the world this year that saw AI agents breaching real commercial and government systems from their test sandboxes.

"The recorded activity involved reading business records, including personal data and confidential material," CERT-In said, adding that none of the organizations affected had detected the access.

The Indian agency said the breaches were revealed in voluntary disclosures by AI model providers.

"In the disclosed cases, the models' actions exceeded the authorization of their assigned tasks," the advisory said.

It did not name the providers or the organizations affected.

Skip next section Air India cancels Saudi Arabia flights until October 20

Air India cancels Saudi Arabia flights until October 20

Air India has canceled its flights to and from Saudi Arabia's cities of Riyadh and Dammam until October 20 amid escalating attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including the recent aerial strikes on the Middle Eastern kingdom's airports. 

"We are closely monitoring developments and continuously assessing the situation to ensure the safe resumption of operations," the Indian flag carrier said Friday on X, adding that passengers impacted by the cancellations were being offered a full refund.

Earlier, IndiGo, India's largest airline, said it was canceling flights to and from Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam and also Medina until October 24.

Meanwhile, India has called on its nationals in Saudi Arabia to not panic and follow instructions from local authorities.

"In the current situation, we have to stay calm and alert and especially in case of an aerial attack, we have to stay indoors," India's envoy to Saudi Arabia, Vipul, said in a video message posted by the embassy.

The ambassador said that one Indian was killed, while 10 others were injured, in an attack on Riyadh airport last Saturday.

Skip next section PM Modi to visit Canada in December

PM Modi to visit Canada in December

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is scheduled to visit Canada from December 11 to 12, the Indian Embassy in Ottawa has announced.

The development comes after Modi and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had a phone call discussing ties between their countries.

"Both the leaders agreed to build on the positive momentum in ties and work towards concrete outcomes in trade, energy, technology, security and people-to-people ties," the Indian high commission in Canada said, referring to the conversation.

Modi had earlier described his talk with Carney as a "warm and productive" one.

"Together, India and Canada are contributing towards a more stable and prosperous world," the Indian leader said.

Earlier this week, Modi also met Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand, who was visiting New Delhi.

Skip next section What do we know about CJP's planned 'Tiranga March'?

What do we know about CJP's planned 'Tiranga March'?

With its previous mass demonstration foiled, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is now campaigning to claim a right to protest — about 600 meters (1,970 feet) away from Jantar Mantar.

Friday's planned protest, featuring the national flag, is scheduled to be held at 5 p.m. local time (1130 UTC) at Central Park in Connaught Place, a prime commercial hub in central Delhi.

"Let's Gather In Large Numbers And Wave Our National Flag. Let's Stand In Support Of Ashutosh and Saurav!" the CJP said, referring to two of the movement's leaders currently being held in detention.

The New Delhi Municipal Corporation, meanwhile, has shut down Central Park for two days, citing "administrative reasons."

Delhi Police said in a statement that prohibitory orders, aimed at maintaining peace and ensuring public safety, were in force in and around Connaught Place.

It called on protesters to not participate in any gathering that violates the orders.

"However, the Delhi Police may consider making arrangements to permit a select group of individuals to gather at a suitable location for the purpose of carrying the national flag and singing the national anthem," Deputy Commissioner of Police Neha Yadav said.

Reports on Friday morning said that security at Connaught Place remains tight. A traffic advisory has been issued for the area.

On Thursday, the Delhi High Court declined to stop the CJP's Connaught Place protest.

"Do we need to take permission to wave our Indian flag?" the 'Cockroach' movement said in a post on X. The CJP posted an emoji of the Indian flag, saying it "belongs to the 1.3 Billion people of this country and not the Delhi police. We will wave it where we want!"

Meanwhile, another "Lehra Do Tiranga" rally called by the CJP in India's financial capital of Mumbai on Friday has received a go-ahead from the city police. The protest is expected to take place at Azad Maidan.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, bringing you our daily digest of all the biggest headlines that have got India talking.

India's 'Cockroach' party is returning to central Delhi with another march almost a week after a protest rally by the youth-led movement was balked by a rare deployment of thousands of security personnel — culminating in mass detentions.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has called on people to gather in large numbers and wave the national flag in Connaught Place in support of its leaders, who were sent to judicial custody for allegedly trespassing at a freshly delisted designated protest site.

The Delhi Police has reiterated that prohibitory orders are in place at the key district and it could allow only a select group of people to gather at a suitable location for the purpose of carrying the flag.

In other news, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Canada in December as the two countries look to shore up bilateral relations.

And India has urged its nationals in Saudi Arabia to stay indoors and follow instructions from local authorities amid a spate of deadly aerial attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels.

Stay tuned for all this and more.
